All elf girls and elf boys receive a map of Elfenland, and they have to visit as many famous towns in Elfenland as possible, using the common types of transportation: dragons, unicorns, giant pigs, elfcycles, troll wagons, magic clouds, ferries and rafts. Thus, an exciting race starts among the elves to find out who will make the best use of the available transportation. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Goal of the game 2 Round overview 3 Travel rules 4 Variant Goal of the game Visiting as many different cities as possible in Elfenland over 4 rounds. Each time you visit a town for the first time, you pick up a Town Piece in your colour. At the end of the 4th round, the player who collected the most Town Pieces wins. Any players having an equal number of Town Pieces are ranked by remaining cards (the more the better). We advise you to play with at least 3 players to best enjoy the game (4 or 5 is even better). A lot of the fun comes from using the Transportation Counters set by other players to optimise one's travels, so the more the merrier! Round overview A round is split into phases: Each player fills their hand up to 8 cards and gets a secret Transportation Counter. One after another, each player chooses a Transportation Counter from the 5 visible or draws from the facedown stack, until each player has taken 3. One after another, each player must plan a travel route by laying a Transportation Counter matching the terrain of the chosen road. This phase goes on until each player has passed consecutively. Each player also owns an Obstacle that they can lay down on a Transportation Counter to increase the cost of travel by an addtional card. Each player only gets one Obstacle in the entire game, use it wisely! One after another, each player travels from town to town. The current position of a player is indicated by the Elf Boot of their color, initially set on the biggest town, Elvenhold. At the end of the round, a player can keep a maximum of 4 cards in hand, and keeps only 1 Transportation counter. All played Transportation counters are then cleared off of the board and a new round begins! Travel rules Players can travel : on the roads on which a Transportation Counter has been set on the rivers on the lakes To travel on a road, a river or a lake, the player needs to pay with the cards in hand the cost matching the terrain of the road and the means of transport used. For example, if the Transportation Counter 'Magic Cloud' has been set on a mountain road, one can travel with just one 'Magic Cloud' card. But if it has been set on a forest or plain road, one needs to pay 2 'Magic Cloud' cards to pass (Note: the 'Magic Cloud' Transportation Counter cannot be placed in the desert, as it's too hot for a Cloud there). Also : To travel a river, you need only 1 'Raft' card to go downriver, but you need 2 to go upriver (look for the small arrow pointing downriver). To cross a lake, you need to pay two 'Raft' cards. If an Obstacle has been set on a road, you need to pay 1 more card of the appropriate type. If you don't have the appropriate cards to travel on a road, you can still pass using a 'Caravan', by paying 3 cards of any type (4 cards if there is an Obstacle on the road). The cards may be any combination of transportation types. Variant In the 'Hometown' variant, each player gets a secret town card at the beginning of the game, telling them which town they have to reach at the end of the 4th round. If they don't manage to get there, they'll lose as many points as the remaining distance they have to travel to get there. This variant gives more tactical depth to the game, as you have to plan each round to the best to get the most Town Pieces while making sure to be able to get to your hometown at the end of the game. Have a good game! Board Game Arena would like to thank Amigo for making it possible to have this game here. 64 elfenla

[Rating: 1/10] I don't mind games that don't give you many options -- in the right circumstances, those games can be fun.  I cannot, however, tolerate a game that systematically nullifies all of your planning, all of your strategy, arbitrarily.  This is the only game I can think of that I would absoltely refuse to play again.

[Rating: 1/10] Essentially plays itself at 3, doesn't work at 2, and can aspire to be worse than ticket to Ride at 4 or 5. - draw cards, draft tiles to help those cards, taking time to hurt your opponent hurts you more.  We kept re reading the rules while we were playing because we assumed we had to be missing something. This game just doesn't have it.

[Rating: 2/10] Reminds me of Candy Land.  I will try it again when my children get a little older.

[Rating: 2/10] (2-6 players) Simple game that just doesn't impress me. Shortest route hacking that feels more like a programming exercise than a fun game.  Supposed to be better with the gold economy expansion but I'm not inclined to try to polish this turd.

[Rating: 2/10] I was excited to try this game because I love its theme. Although the moving system only SUCKS. The game SUCKS. I SUCK in this game (I think I came second in our four-player game, but it still felt so).  Ok, I'll probably have a replay after a couple of decades but while waiting for it, I'll spend my time with better games and remember how this one SUCKED.    Ok, sorry about the number of those words ^^;; Well, the art was kinda beautiful. Despite that, no more of this please...

[Rating: 2/10] One of my least favorite games.  The play was tedious, limited, uninspiring, and very very loosely themed.  That little peg is an elf prince?  riiiiiight.  Might as well have been a serial killer or the pony express.  I love Ticket to Ride but will outright refuse to play this one.
